paras.text: LSAT Question Types & Fallacies, Audio Lecture

This chapter has two halves, and they do different jobs. The first half is what the actual LSAT's Logical Reasoning section is built to test, as LSAC itself describes it. The second half is a catalog of nine recurring informal fallacies, the kind that show up in a GC contract, a claims denial letter, a DFS argument, or a sales pitch, whether or not any test ever asks you about them. Keep the two halves straight in your head, because they answer different questions. One describes a test. The other describes reasoning you'll meet for the rest of your life.

Let's start with something most LSAT material gets a little dishonest about. LSAC itself, on its own official pages, does not label its questions with names like necessary assumption, strengthen, weaken, flaw, or parallel reasoning. Go read LSAC's own page, and the one on LawHub, which is LSAC's own prep platform, and here is what you actually find. LSAC says Logical Reasoning questions assess your ability to analyze, critically evaluate, and complete arguments. Then it lists ten specific skills. Recognizing the parts of an argument and their relationships. Recognizing similarities and differences between patterns of reasoning. Drawing well supported conclusions. Reasoning by analogy. Recognizing misunderstandings or points of disagreement. Determining how additional evidence affects an argument. Detecting assumptions made by particular arguments. Identifying and applying principles or rules. Identifying flaws in arguments. Identifying explanations. That's it. Ten skills, in plain language. LSAC even says directly that you will not need to know the meaning of a term like ad hominem to do well on the test.

So where do all those familiar names come from, the ones every prep book and tutor throws around? They're an industry convention. Test prep companies took LSAC's ten skills and built a shorthand vocabulary on top of them, because it's useful to have a name for a pattern you'll see over and over. One source I checked counts twenty two distinct named sub-types. Another says the count runs anywhere from eight to twenty two, depending on how a given company groups them. There is no single official count, because there is no official list. What I'm giving you below is that conventional shorthand, cross checked against an established source, mapped back to the specific LSAC skill each one actually drills. Treat the LSAC skill description as the solid ground and the name as a useful label sitting on top of it.

One more fact before the types themselves, because it matters and people get it wrong constantly. The LSAT is scored on a scale from 120, the lowest possible score, to 180, the highest. There is no deduction for a wrong answer. Your raw count of correct answers gets converted onto that scale. This track is not going to tell you it raises your actual LSAT score by some number of points, because that's not something anyone can honestly claim without running you through LSAC's own instrument. What this track does is teach you the underlying reasoning skill, the one that also happens to be exactly what you need to read a contract clause, a denial letter, or a betting argument correctly. The skill transfers. A specific point total is not something I'm going to promise you.
Now the types themselves, grouped the way they naturally pair up.

Necessary and sufficient assumption. An assumption is something the argument needs that was never actually stated. A necessary assumption is the floor: without it the argument falls apart, but having it doesn't guarantee the conclusion. A sufficient assumption is the ceiling: add it, and the conclusion is now fully locked in, no gaps left. Here's a restoration example. A GC bids a mold job assuming the crew can finish in three days. The necessary assumption buried in there is something like, nothing behind this wall will require extra containment time. If that's false, the bid is dead. But even if it's true, three days still isn't guaranteed; other things could slow the job down. A sufficient assumption would be much stronger: this exact crew has never once exceeded three days on an identical scope, documented across every past job. Add that, and the three day claim is airtight.

Question for you. I'll describe a claim, and I want you to tell me whether it sounds necessary or sufficient. An adjuster says a water loss is covered because it came from a plumbing failure, not surface water. The necessary assumption is that the policy doesn't have language sweeping plumbing failures back under an exclusion anyway. Is that claim, by itself, strong enough to guarantee coverage, or just something the argument needs without guaranteeing anything?

It's necessary, not sufficient. It keeps the argument from immediately failing, but it doesn't by itself prove coverage; you'd still need to check the whole policy for other exclusions and conditions before the conclusion is locked in.

Strengthen and weaken. Both questions give you a new fact and ask how it changes the argument, without proving or disproving the conclusion outright. A strengthener makes the stated premises support the conclusion more. A weakener makes them support it less. Picture a DFS argument: this running back has had twenty plus touches in three straight games, so he smashes value tonight. A strengthener would be learning tonight's opponent has the league's worst run defense; that makes the established pattern more likely to actually convert into points. A weakener would be learning the starting quarterback from those three games just landed on injured reserve; now the whole offensive situation that produced those touches might not repeat.

Flaw. This one asks you to name the actual logical defect in an argument's reasoning, and it doesn't care whether the conclusion happens to be true in the real world. A conclusion can be correct and the argument for it can still be garbage. Sales pitch example: our last three jobs in your zip code passed inspection first try, so yours will too. The flaw is generalizing from a tiny, self selected sample to guarantee an outcome on a different job with different conditions. That's the same defect as one of the fallacies coming up in the second half, which tells you something: a lot of flaw questions are really just a named fallacy wearing a different hat.

Must be true, sometimes called inference, and its flip side, must be false. An inference question gives you facts and asks what's guaranteed by those facts alone, no outside assumptions allowed. Notice the direction is the reverse of an assumption question: assumption questions ask what the argument needs; inference questions ask what the stated facts already lock in. Claims example: a policy says the dwelling limit is three hundred thousand dollars and requires coverage of at least actual cash value at time of loss. From those two facts, you can only conclude the payout on a total loss will be at least the dwelling's actual cash value. You cannot conclude the insurer pays exactly three hundred thousand; that would need an extra assumption about what full replacement actually costs.

Parallel reasoning, and its cousin, parallel flaw. These strip out the subject and ask you to match an argument's abstract structure to a new argument on a totally different topic. Parallel flaw does the same thing but the structure being matched is broken, and you're hunting for the answer that repeats the identical mistake. Trading example: if the Fed cuts rates, bond yields fall; yields fell today, so the Fed must have cut rates. That's a logical error called affirming the consequent, covered formally in the first domain of this track. A parallel flaw answer on weather would be: if it rains, the field gets muddy; the field is muddy, so it must have rained. Same mistake, different clothes: both ignore that something else could've caused the same effect.

Principle questions run in two directions. Find the rule gives you a specific situation and asks which general principle would justify it. Find the application gives you a general principle and asks which specific situation it actually covers. Contract example: a change order clause says any scope change over ten percent of contract value needs written sign off before work proceeds. Find the application would hand you five job site scenarios and ask which one actually triggers that clause. Find the rule would describe a contractor who stopped and got signatures before a big change, and ask what general policy that behavior is consistent with.

Paradox, sometimes called resolve, reconcile, or explain. Two facts both seem true, and they appear to contradict each other. The job is to find the one new fact that lets both stand without anybody being wrong or dishonest. Claims example: an adjuster inspects a roof from the ground and finds no storm damage; the homeowner's own contractor climbs up and finds three cracked tabs from the same storm. The resolving fact might simply be that the adjuster never actually got on the roof. Nobody lied. The methods were just different.

Main point, or main conclusion. This asks which answer restates the argument's actual bottom line, as opposed to a premise, a side point, or an opposing view the author is knocking down. The trap is a true, forceful sounding sentence from the passage that's actually just a premise supporting the real conclusion, not the conclusion itself. If a pitch says, our crew finished in record time, we used efficient scheduling, therefore we're the best choice for your next job, the conclusion is that last clause. The record time and the scheduling are the evidence offered for it, not the point itself.

Method of reasoning, and a close cousin, point at issue. Method of reasoning asks you to describe, in the abstract, how an argument is built; for instance, by ruling out every competing explanation but one. Point at issue gives you two speakers and asks what they actually disagree about, which is often narrower than it first looks. Picture a public adjuster and a carrier adjuster who both agree a job is multi trade, but argue only over whether a general contractor was reasonably likely needed. The point at issue is that one specific sentence, not the broader multi trade fact they already agree on.

That covers the first half. Now the second half: nine fallacies, pure formal logic, true by definition, and worth getting exactly right because a wrong definition sounds just as confident as a right one.

Correlation versus causation. Two things happening together doesn't prove one caused the other; a third factor or plain coincidence can produce the same pattern. A bettor who notices a kicker's accuracy rose every game the team wore their away jersey, and concludes the jersey caused it, is ignoring that those away games also happened to be against weaker defenses. That's the real explanation, not the jersey.

Circular reasoning. The conclusion just restates one of the premises in different words, so nothing has actually been proven. This contractor is the best because nobody does better work than they do. Best and nobody does better work are the same claim, said twice.

Equivocation. A key term quietly shifts meaning partway through the argument. A policy excludes flood; the adjuster uses flood to mean any rising water in the denial letter, while the policy's own endorsement defines flood narrowly as a general surface water event hitting multiple properties. Sliding between those two meanings to deny a single property plumbing leak is equivocation.

Composition and division, which run in opposite directions. Composition assumes what's true of each part must be true of the whole. Division assumes what's true of the whole must be true of each part. A crew finishing a job in record time doesn't mean every single technician on it is individually fast; one could've been slow while others covered. That's division.

Ad hominem. Attacking the person instead of the argument, as if the attack itself disproves the claim. Don't listen to that public adjuster's estimate, he's just chasing a commission. That might be true and it's a fair thing to know, but it says nothing about whether his measurements and pricing are actually correct. It only becomes the fallacy when the personal attack stands in for an actual rebuttal.

False dichotomy. Presenting only two options when more exist. Either you sign today at this price or the check expires and you get nothing. Most claims checks don't expire on a sales deadline, and other bids, more time, and a public adjuster are all real options the pitch is hiding.

Unrepresentative or biased sampling. Drawing a big conclusion from a sample too small or too skewed to support it. A trader who backtests a strategy only on five bull market months, never touching a down month, and calls it proven, hasn't tested the conditions that would actually challenge the claim.

Appeal to authority. Treating a claim as true just because someone with a title said it, regardless of whether their expertise actually covers the claim. My insurance agent said this isn't covered. An agent sells policies; they don't adjudicate coverage disputes. Their opinion isn't the same as the policy language or a court's reading of it.

Slippery slope. Arguing one small step guarantees a chain of increasingly extreme outcomes, without showing each link is actually likely. If you don't let us start mitigation today, the mold spreads through the whole house, then you lose the structure, then you have nowhere to live. Each step is asserted, never shown. Naming this fallacy doesn't mean mold risk is never real in a given case; it means this particular chain wasn't demonstrated, only asserted.

Last question before we recap. You're looking at a claims letter that says: our senior adjuster, with twenty years of experience, has reviewed this file and confirms it falls under the exclusion, so the denial stands. Nothing about the actual policy language or the facts of your loss is discussed. Name the fallacy.

Appeal to authority. Years of experience is not nothing, but citing a title instead of the actual policy language and the facts of the loss is exactly the pattern: treating the claim as settled because of who said it, not what they showed.

Here's the recap. Half one: LSAC itself describes ten skills, not named question types; the names you've learned are a useful, widely shared convention sitting on top of those skills, and the LSAT's own scale runs 120 to 180 with no penalty for a wrong guess. Necessary versus sufficient assumption: floor versus ceiling. Strengthen and weaken move the needle without proving or disproving. Flaw grades the logic, not the real world truth. Must be true locks in only what the stated facts actually guarantee. Parallel reasoning matches structure across unrelated topics. Principle runs rule to application or application to rule. Paradox reconciles two true but seemingly conflicting facts. Main point is the conclusion, not the evidence for it. Method of reasoning and point at issue describe how an argument is built and exactly where two people actually disagree.

Half two: nine fallacies, correlation versus causation, circular reasoning, equivocation, composition and division, ad hominem, false dichotomy, unrepresentative sampling, appeal to authority, and slippery slope, each one a recurring, nameable defect you'll run into in a contract, a denial letter, or a pitch, whether a test ever asks you about it or not. Spot the pattern once, and you'll see it everywhere after.
